                            UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                        NUCLEAR REGULATORY COMMISSION

 In the Matter of:                              §

 Long Mott Energy, LLC                          §

                                                §
 (Long Mott Generating Station)                 §

   COMMENT OF EDWIN LYMAN, Ph.D. IN OPPOSITION TO THE LONG MOTT
           ENERGY CONSTRUCTION PERMIT APPLICATION

I, Dr. Edwin Lyman, declare as follows:

1. My name is Edwin Lyman. The information in this statement is based on my personal
   experience and my review of publicly available information.

Background

2. I am the Director of Nuclear Power Safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) in
   Washington, DC, and I have been employed at UCS since 2003. I earned a doctorate degree in
   physics from Cornell University in 1992. I have over three decades of experience in nuclear
   power safety and security, working as a postdoctoral research associate at Princeton
   University’s Center for Energy and Environmental Studies (now the Science and Global
   Security Program) and serving as the president of the Nuclear Control Institute before I joined
   UCS. I have published articles and letters regarding those issues in journals and magazines
   including Science, Nature, The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, Science and Global Security,
   Arms Control Today, Nuclear Engineering International, New Scientist and Energy and
   Environmental Science. I am a co-author (with David Lochbaum and Susan Q. Stranahan) of
   the book Fukushima: The Story of a Nuclear Disaster (The New Press, 2014). I am a member
   of the Institute of Nuclear Materials Management and the American Nuclear Society, and I
   have testified before Congress and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and published articles
   in several journals and magazines about nuclear power. In 2018 I was awarded the Leo Szilard
   Lectureship Award from the American Physical Society for my work on nuclear safety and
   security. I have also served as a qualified expert witness for intervenors in several NRC
   adjudicatory proceedings.
 3. Review of Long Mott Energy, LLC’s Application

4. In 2025 to early 2026 I was engaged as a technical consultant by San Antonio Bay Estuarine
   Waterkeeper (“Waterkeeper”) for purposes of reviewing the Long Mott Generating Station’s
   (“Long Mott”) Construction Permit Application (“CPA” or “LM-CPA”) and identifying issues
   of concern that may be relevant to Waterkeeper and its members.

5. To that end, I have reviewed Long Mott’s CPA. I am familiar with and have reviewed
   applicable NRC regulations, policies, and guidance documents.

6. I assisted Waterkeeper with the preparation of their Contention 1, which addresses the
   adequacy of LM-CPA’s proposed functional containment.

7. On January 22, 2026, the ASLB incorrectly rejected Waterkeeper’s Contention 1. Here, I
   restate my objection to approval of the LM-CPA, supplemented with updated information, for
   the Commission’s consideration.

Contention

8. The LM-CPA seeks NRC approval under 10 CFR Part 50 for an alternative, “functional”
   containment instead of a conventional, low-leakage, physical containment structure.

9. 10 CFR Part 50 does not contain a definition of “functional containment,” nor does it have any
   provisions that specify what it is or what its performance requirements are. References to
   “functional containment” are scattered among various guidance documents but a coherent and
   comprehensive set of recommended performance criteria for functional containments for Part
   50 applicants does not exist.

10. In contrast, the performance requirements for a conventional containment are specified in
   General Design Criterion (GDC) 16 in Appendix A of 10 CFR Part 50: “Reactor containment
   and associated systems shall be provided to establish an essentially leak-tight barrier against
   the uncontrolled release of radioactivity to the environment and to assure that the containment
   design conditions important to safety are not exceeded for as long as postulated accident
   conditions require.” The GDCs are only regulatory requirements for “water-cooled” nuclear
   plants but are “generally applicable” to other plant types and are “intended to provide
   guidance” for establishing the principal design criteria (PDCs) for such units.



                                             Page 2
 11. The NRC staff adapted the Modular High-Temperature Gas-Cooled Reactor Design Criterion
   (“MHTGR-DC”) 16, “Containment Design,” from the Advanced Reactor Design Criterion
   (ARDC) 16 in Regulatory Guide 1.232, Rev. 0, “Guidance for Developing Principal Design
   Criteria for Non-Light-Water Reactors” (April 2018): “Containment design: A reactor
   functional containment, consisting of multiple barriers internal and/or external to the reactor
   and its cooling system, shall be provided to control the release of radioactivity to the
   environment and to ensure that the functional containment design conditions important to
   safety are not exceeded for as long as postulated accident conditions require.”

12. The NRC staff’s rationale in RG 1.232 for modifying the Advanced Reactor Design Criterion
   (ARDC) 16 for MHTGRs specifically cited the condition that “approval of the proposed
   approach to functional containment for the MHTGR concept, with its emphasis on passive
   safety features and radionuclide retention within the fuel over a broad spectrum of off- normal
   conditions, would necessitate that the required fuel particle performance capabilities be
   demonstrated with a high degree of certainty.” RG 1.232, App. C, p. C-9 (ML17325A611)
   (emphasis added).

13. This condition is consistent with the common understanding that TRISO fuel performance is
   the most important component of the safety case underlying the functional containment. In the
   words of ACRS member Walt Kirchner, “the “whole functional containment hangs on the
   performance of this [Xe-100 TRISO] fuel” (ACRS New Reactors Subcommittee Meeting,
   September 2, 2026).

14. In the LM-CPA, an alternative to MHTGR-DC 16 was proposed: “PDC RFDC 16 - Functional
   Containment Design: The design of the reactor fuel particles and pebbles shall provide barriers
   as part of the reactor functional containment to control the release of radioactivity to the
   environment to ensure that the functional containment design limit is not exceeded during
   design basis events and design basis accidents.” But as is clear from the discussion in the
   August 2023 Xe-100 Licensing Topical Report on Principal Design Criteria, Rev. 3
   ML26048A745), these changes were made to align with specific terms used in the application,
   and LM made no suggestion that disputed the underlying technical basis stated in R.G. 1.232
   for MHTGR-DC. In fact, LM made a change to clarify that the functional containment has a
   design limit that “cannot be exceeded” (emphasis ours). This choice of words is certainly



                                             Page 3
    consistent with the notion that fuel performance, and in particular the quantitative
   determinations of radionuclide releases under all design basis event and design basis accident
   conditions, must be determined with a high degree of certainty, to ensure that functional
   containment design limits are not exceeded. Thus the experimental demonstration of the
   performance of prototypical Xe-100 fuel, including accurate measurement of radionuclide
   releases under all design-basis accident and event conditions, is critical to establishing that the
   functional containment meets NRC regulations, as well as LM’s own RFDC-16. As the Rev.
   2 LM-CPA PSAR states (p. 13.3-3), "testing is needed to confirm that burnup, fast fluence,
   and temperature outside the validated range from previous testing will not challenge the fuel’s
   ability to meet its RSFs [Reactor Safety Functions]”—namely, to “retain radionuclides in fuel
   particles and pebbles.”

15. The close interrelationship between Xe-100 fuel performance and the proposed LM functional
   containment calls into question whether the NRC has sufficient information at this stage to
   approve the LM-CPA. The reason is simple: the necessary fuel qualification datasets needed
   to demonstrate that the functional containment design limits cannot be exceeded are not
   currently available and thus are not contained in the LM-CPA. The experimental fuel
   qualification program now underway will not provide all the necessary data until Fall 2030
   (PSAR, Rev. 2, Table 6.4.2-1). Should the NRC approve the LM-CPA, construction is likely
   to be well underway by the time the critical fuel performance data is available.

16. The NRC should not allow construction to proceed based on the current design, which lacks a
   conventional physical containment, without the necessary information to validate that the
   functional containment alternative will meet regulatory requirements. Should the data
   emerging from the fuel qualification program reveal that the assumptions about fuel
   performance in the LM-CPA are inaccurate and non-conservative, then the regulatory basis for
   approving the functional containment will be undermined. Although the NRC maintains that
   LM will be proceeding at its own risk should it begin construction under these circumstances,
   I do not believe, given the enormous cost and schedule implications, that there is any realistic
   possibility that the NRC would later order the design to be changed mid-construction and that
   the project be backfitted with a physical containment, no matter what the data shows. My
   concern is that the NRC may instead conduct a so-called “risk-informed” operability



                                              Page 4
    assessment to justify not requiring such a retrofit. I note that Executive Order 14300 stipulates
   that the NRC “establish stringent thresholds for circumstances in which the NRC may demand
   changes to reactor design once construction is underway,” putting pressure on the agency to
   avoid requiring such changes. Consequently, to provide public confidence that the NRC will
   not hesitate to act should the experimental evidence demand it, any CP issued by the NRC for
   the LM project should contain legally enforceable license conditions that the design be
   modified to later accommodate addition of a physical containment, and that the NRC will
   require addition of a physical containment should the fuel qualification program demonstrate
   that functional containment design limits may be exceeded.

17. I also note that no matter what the experimental program may reveal, the safety performance
   provided by the functional containment can never be assured to the same degree as that of a
   physical containment. Leak-tightness of a physical containment—a property that is essential
   for assuring compliance with design-basis accident safety requirements in 10 CFR 50.34, can
   be measured and controlled with the procedures required in Appendix J of 10 CFR Part 50.
   There is no comparable set of requirements for the performance of fuel as a primary component
   of a functional containment for which compliance can be so clearly demonstrated.

18. Based on my professional judgment and my review of the LM-CPA and relevant NRC
   regulations and guidance documents, it is my opinion that the LM-CPA fails to demonstrate
   that the functional containment design limits “cannot” be exceeded in all design basis accidents
   and design basis events. An explanation of the various bases for my opinion are detailed below.

19. By any reasonable standard, the LM-CPA does not demonstrate “the required fuel performance
   capabilities … with a high degree of certainty.” The plain reason is that an evaluation model
   validated with the experimental information necessary for determining fuel performance
   capabilities and developing accurate mechanistic source terms, which are essential for
   evaluating the performance of the functional containment, is not available at the present time
   and will not be available until commercial-scale fuel produced under prototypical conditions
   has been fully tested over a sufficiently “broad spectrum of off-normal conditions.” The
   necessary information that is absent includes (1) demonstrated fuel fabrication defect rates and
   (2) radionuclide release fractions from as-manufactured fuel at the peak temperatures predicted




                                             Page 5
    in certain licensing basis events (including certain design-basis accidents) in the LM-CPA,
   which have not been experimentally determined.

20. Thus, the LM-CPA fails to demonstrate with reasonable assurance that the proposed functional
   containment will control the release of radioactivity to the environment under all “postulated
   accident conditions” and thereby does not fulfill the safety design objective of meeting “10
   CFR 50.34 … offsite dose requirements at the plant’s exclusion area boundary (EAB) with
   margins,” as stated in RG. 1.232, Appendix C, MHTGR-DC 16, which is one of the design
   limits that the LM-CPA commits to in its revised RFDC-16.

21. Therefore, to meet the letter and the intent of MHTGR-DC 16, the Xe-100 design referenced
   in the LM-CPA must include a conventional, essentially leak-tight containment structure to
   ensure compliance with 10 CFR 50.34. This is consistent with the recommendation made by
   NRC staff in its 1995 draft MHGTR preapplication safety review that a prototype MHTGR
   with a low-leakage containment should be considered if the “necessary design and quality of
   the fuel to meet the performance objectives” has not been demonstrated. See Draft Copy of
   Preapplication-Safety Evaluation Report (PSER) on the Modular High-Temperature Gas-
   Cooled Reactor (MHTGR) (March 26, 1996) (ML052780519).

22. Below are the various reasons that, in my professional judgment, the mechanistic source terms
   in the LM-CPA’s proposed functional containment demonstration fail to meet the minimum
   criteria for adequacy:

   Computer code is still under development

23. The LM-CPA utilizes a computer code known as XSTERM to develop the mechanistic source
   terms utilized in the modeling of the dose consequences of Xe-100 accidents. The code is
   referenced in the X-Energy Licensing Topical Report (MST TR) “Mechanistic Source Term
   Approach, Revision 3” (non-public version), which is incorporated by reference in the LM-
   CPA. However, the NRC staff state that although the MST TR “provides a reasonable plan for
   the development of the MST methodology,” the staff “makes no conclusions regarding the
   acceptability of the models in XSTERM for the MST analyses of the Xe-100 because …
   models within XSTERM are still under development” (Staff presentation to ACRS
   subcommittee, September 1-2, 2026).



                                            Page 6
    No manufacturing defect data from fuel to justify assumptions

24. The ACRS letter on the X-Energy MST LR states: “The source term from TRISO fuel in a
   high temperature gas-cooled reactor is a strong function of the initial level of manufacturing
   defects (heavy metal contamination, SiC defects), the in-service failures under irradiation, and
   the incremental failures during postulated accidents. Because of the importance to the overall
   functional containment strategy, the initial fuel failure fractions used in the X-energy safety
   analysis approach must bound actual manufacturing data.” ACRS Letter at 4.

25. However, validation of the as-manufactured defect rate assumptions is currently impossible.
   The reason is that the facility where the TRISO pebbles for the LM project will be fabricated—
   the TRISO-X plant proposed for construction in Oak Ridge, TN—does not yet exist. Moreover,
   even if X-Energy’s projection that it hopes to produce its first pebble in December 2027 (see
   https://www.exchangemonitor.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/bell-smrs.pdf) is realized, it
   is not likely that statistically meaningful data on production-scale defect rates would be
   available for several years after that—that is, long after the NRC is scheduled to complete its
   review of the LM-CPA and the functional containment approach.

26. Such data is crucial, though, because of evidence that the X-Energy MST model assumes
   particle defect rates “significantly lower” than what was ever achieved in fuel production
   campaigns in both Germany and the United States, according to ACRS member Dr. David
   Petti (ACRS X-Energy subcommittee transcript, June 3, 2025, pp. 247-249, ML25192A240).
   Thus, to justify the use of such low failure rates, LM has the burden of demonstrating them
   with the actual process that will be used to manufacture the fuel.

27. Again, the NRC’s assumption is that the fuel specification assumed in the LM-CPA will be
   met by the fuel ultimately produced by TRISO-X, and if it is not, then it will not allow the
   plant to operate. However, for the same reason that I am skeptical the NRC would make a
   decision to require retrofitting with a physical containment, I doubt that the NRC would hold
   LM to the fuel specification it committed to should the TRISO-X facility not be able to meet
   the spec, thus endangering the entire, multibillion dollar investment.



   Assumptions underlying DLOFC are invalid



                                             Page 7
 28. Moreover, assumptions made in the LM-CPA about the performance of its fuel in support of
   the development of MSTs have not been validated, based on the maximum fuel temperatures
   and sustained peak temperatures that are achievable and even anticipated at the plant. Thus,
   the LM-CPA analyses of Design Basis Accidents (“DBAs”) including depressurized loss of
   forced circulation (“DLOFC”) supporting the adequacy of the functional containment to meet
   regulatory requirements are unverified and invalid, in my professional judgment.

29. The LM-CPA analysis of the “extreme case” “depressurized loss of forced circulation” event,
   or DLOFC, which occurs in the course of a number of the DBAs evaluated, results in maximum
   fuel temperatures approaching 2000°C for nearly two days, and sustains peak temperatures of
   over 1800°C for a period of several days after that. This is well outside of the bounds
   established by the LM TRISO fuel qualification TR from the experimental database for TRISO
   uranium oxycarbide (UCO) fuel. Thus, any assumptions made in the LM-CPA about the
   performance of its fuel under such conditions that support the development of MSTs have not
   been validated.

30. It is clear from the literature on TRISO fuel and MHTGR safety analyses that a peak
   temperature of 1600°C is typically set as the bounding condition for the outcome of the
   DLOFC, which is the most limiting design-basis accident for this class of reactors. This is
   because diffusion of most fission products through the multiple layers of the TRISO fuel is not
   expected to occur for intact particles held below this temperature for less than about 200 hours.
   See Petti, Hobbins, Lowry, and Gougar, Representative Source Terms and the Influence of
   Reactor Attributes on Functional Containment in Modular High-Temperature Gas-Cooled
   Reactors,         Nuclear     Technology,        184(2),       181–197        (available      at:
   https://doi.org/10.13182/NT184-181).

31. However, as the temperature increases above 1600°C, TRISO particle failures steadily
   increase, and can increase by an order of magnitude or more at 1800°C, increasing some fission
   product release fractions by two orders of magnitude or greater. High Temperature Gas Cooled
   Reactor Fuels and Materials, IAEA TECDOC-1645, at 85-93 (2010). Above 1800°C, test data
   is sparse (and non-existent for the Xe-100 UCO TRISO fuel), but a 2022 US national
   laboratory study notes that “accident condition failures are very sensitive to increases in
   temperature above 1800°C since the SiC [silicon carbide] layer chemically decomposes as it



                                             Page 8
    approaches and rises above 2000°C. Particles should be conservatively expected to eventually
   release all volatile and certain diffusive fission products somewhat above this sustained
   [1800°C] heat soak temperature.” Coles et al., Parametric Study of Factors that Affect
   Calculated Dose from TRISO Fueled Microreactor Transportation Accident, Pacific
   Northwest National Laboratory/ Idaho National Laboratory, at 17 (Nov. 2022) (available at:
   https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1922640).

32. Despite this lack of data for the fission product releases from X-Energy fuel at these extreme
   temperatures, the LM-CPA assumes a relatively low overall increase in failure fractions for
   DBAs involving DLOFCs. For example, by comparing the total activity released in the Seismic
   DBA (which is the most limiting DBA with less than a factor of 2 margin to the 25 rem
   regulatory limit), to the initial isotopic inventory for a radionuclide such as cesium-137, the
   increase in release fraction is about a factor of about 40, whereas the limited German data
   (which is for uranium dioxide; similar data does not exist for UCO) shows an increase of a
   factor of around 1000 at 1800°C compared to 1600°C (IAEA TECDOC-1645 at 92). Thus,
   there is considerable uncertainty and the possibility exists that the MST and radiological
   consequences for the Seismic DBA are significantly underestimated.

   Methodology for calculation of the core radionuclide inventory is unreliable

33. Although the LM-CPA lacks sufficient detail to make a definitive conclusion, based on my
   review of the limited data contained therein, the methodology for calculation of the core
   radionuclide inventory appears to have large uncertainties and possibly even errors that may
   result in an underestimate of the total radionuclide inventory and hence the MSTs used to
   justify the adequacy of the functional containment.

34. The initial isotopic inventory in the LM-CPA that is used to develop the mechanistic source
   terms for DBA consequence analysis is presented in Table 3.3-2 of the LM-CPA PSAR (PSAR
   at 3.3-3). The column of values for DBAs, which are interpreted as the fraction of the core
   inventory in the helium pressure boundary (which includes the buildup of plated out fission
   products over the 60 effective full power year core lifetime) incorporates a “maximum
   allowable” fuel failure fraction of 1x10-4. Because of the different components making up the
   reported inventory, it is not possible to extrapolate from these values to the total radionuclide
   inventory in the core without having access to proprietary details about the evaluation model.


                                             Page 9
 35. Even so, some of the total core inventory values can be extracted, and from those, one can see
   that they are smaller than those provided in several other references describing very similar
   reactor designs at equilibrium. For example, iodine isotopes that leak out of defective particles
   are not believed to be retained in the graphite pebbles, and hence the iodine reported should be
   equivalent to the quantity reported in the helium pressure boundary (Petti et al. 2013). Thus,
   for example, the total core inventory of iodine-134 (I-134) would be 1x10 4 times the inventory
   reported in the LM-CPA, or 7.75x1014 becquerels (Bq).

36. However, a recent study of the 250-MWt HTR-PM Chinese pebble-bed HTGR, using a new
   model for inventory calculations calculated an inventory of 6.1x10 17 Bq of I-134 at
   equilibrium. Raza et al., Development of radionuclide inventory and fission product release
   calculation model and its application to HTR-PM, Annals of Nuclear Energy, Vol. 212 (March
   2025) (available at: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306454924007370).
   Since the core inventory of I-134, a short-lived fission product, is roughly proportional to
   power level, this would correspond to about 1.3x10 17 Bq for the 200 MWt Xe-100—over one
   hundred times greater than the value in the LM-CPA. Given that several other sources that
   estimate the total equilibrium core inventory are consistent with the values in Raza et al., the
   LM-CPA appears to be an outlier.

37. Similar analyses for other fission product values reported in the LM-CPA also show that they
   are underestimated compared to other references. Even greater discrepancies occur for noble
   gas fission products. For example, Raza et al. calculates an inventory of 2.9x1017 Bq for
   krypton-89 (Kr-89), another short-lived fission product that is not retained in graphite and
   should be proportional to power level. But the Xe-100 Kr-89 inventory is only 1.62x10 13 Bq—
   four orders of magnitude too small. And discrepancies are also apparent for longer lived
   isotopes such as Cs-137. Raza et al. calculates a core inventory of 2x1016 Bq, which is 1.6x1016
   Bq when scaled to 200 MWt. The Xe-100 Cs-137 core inventory should be greater than this,
   as the assumed maximum burnup of 168 GWd/MTU (MST LTR at 13) is nearly twice that
   assumed for the HTR-PM in Raza, et al. However, based on the attenuation factor of 5 cited
   for Cs-137 in Petti et al., this would imply an Xe-100 Cs-137 inventory less than 5.3x1015 Bq.

38. And there are also inexplicably missing isotopes in the LM-CPA list, most notably strontium-
   89 (Sr-89), which Raza et al. find has a higher activity than Sr-90 does.



                                             Page 10
 39. Thus, in my professional judgment, these uncertainties and potential inaccuracies in the core
   inventory are cause for an additional lack of assurance that the MST calculations supporting
   the adequacy of the functional containment are conservative.

   Other deficiencies

40. There are only very limited experimental measurements of iodine and tellurium releases in
   temperature transients (ACRS subcommittee transcript at 185). As these isotopes are
   significant contributors to offsite dose, this lack of data introduces significant uncertainty into
   the MST calculations supporting the adequacy of functional containment.

41. The AGR program test data for UCO fuel is only available for compacts rather than the pebble
   fuel forms that the Xe-100 will use. This has been noted as a significant limitation in the use
   of AGR data for assessing the effectiveness of the Xe-100 fuel matrix as a component of the
   functional containment. See X Energy, LLC – Safety Evaluation of XE-100 Topical Report,
   TRISO-X Pebble Fuel Qualification Methodology, Rev. 3, p. 6 (March 29, 2023).

42. There has been no testing of sufficiently representative fuel manufactured at a commercial
   scale. As discussed below, X-Energy’s plan to conduct such testing at Idaho National
   Laboratory is highly unlikely to yield results in time to inform the NRC’s decision on the LM-
   CPA’s proposed functional containment.

43. There is no experimental data available on steam ingress and its effect on the Xe-100 core.
   This phenomenon could have a significant impact on the MST used to assess the adequacy of
   functional containment (ACRS letter at 5). The Department of Energy is constructing a furnace
   to conduct such tests, but the schedule is uncertain, and again, it is unclear when useful data
   will be available for incorporation into the MST model.

   LM-CPA does not address limitations regarding Fuel Qualification Topical Report

44. The LM-CPA references the X-Energy Fuel Qualification Topical Report, Revision 3
   (ML22216A179). The staff approved this Report in March 2023 subject to three limitations
   and conditions:

           1. Applicant’s referencing the Technical Report (TR) should provide a justification
              for releases from defect particles, contamination in the fuel matrix, and diffusion of
              volatile radionuclides in addition to the intact particle failure fraction derived from


                                              Page 11
                the testing to be used in a future licensing application. In effect, this methodology
               forms a portion of the fuel qualification for the final reactor fuel form, but not the
               entirety of the fuel qualification process for the performance of the fuel (e.g., cover
               the aspects cited above or the more comprehensive list of fuel qualification areas in
               NUREG-2246).”

           2. This approval is limited to the plan to test TRISO fuel and the operational envelope
               (temperature, burnup, and environmental conditions) outlined in the TR.
               Applicant’s referencing the TR should provide a set of fuel specifications and
               demonstrate how fuel to be used in the reactor will meet these specifications. Future
               licensing submittals will be needed to qualify the fuel for the totality of the
               operational regime, including but not limited to transient accident conditions and
               mechanical effects to the extent that these are not incorporated within the scope of
               the TR.

           3. An applicant referencing the TR is subject to the limitations and conditions
               associated with the approved EPRI TRISO TR.

45. For reasons including those discussed above, the LM-CPA does not conform to the staff’s
   limitations. X-Energy’s plan to address this problem is through a testing program which it
   projects will not be completed until Fall 2030 and is not testing prototypical fuel (for example,
   the pebbles are smaller than the actual Xe-100 fuel). Given the current unavailability of as-
   manufactured fuel from the yet-to-be-built TRISO-X facility, as well as the length of time such
   tests have taken historically to yield data, it is not clear that LM can complete its testing on the
   compressed timetable it has presented in Rev. 2 of the PSAR, and it is unclear whether useful
   results from such testing will be available by the time the operating license application is
   submitted, much less by the time the NRC has committed to make a decision on the LM-CPA.
   By way of comparison, the Advanced Gas-cooled Reactor (“AGR”) program at INL took more
   than 10 years from fabrication of the fuel through irradiation and post-irradiation examination.
   Demkowicz, AGR Program TRISO Fuel Topical Report Dialog, slide 7 (Feb. 2022) (available
   at: https://inldigitallibrary.inl.gov/sites/sti/sti/Sort_57185.pdf).

46. In my professional judgment, it is highly unlikely that the LM-CPA will comply with 10 C.F.R.
   § 50.34(a)(8). This is because the latest date for completion of construction cited in the LM-


                                               Page 12
    CPA is 2033 (LM-CPA, Part I-1). The highly abbreviated schedule presented in the PSAR
   Rev. 2 for irradiation, testing, and post-irradiation examination, which is far shorter the actual
   timetable of the AGR program, is not reasonably achievable.

47. Similarly, based on the above discussion, in my professional judgment, the LM-CPA simply
   does not demonstrate that the proposed Xe-100 functional containment will provide adequate
   protection of public health and safety and does not comply with the requirements of 10 C.F.R.
   § 50.34(a)(4). This is because the adequacy of the functional containment, which is dependent
   on the adequacy of the MST determination, has not been demonstrated. In the absence of such
   a determination, the reactor design must be modified to include a conventional, nearly leak-
   tight, physical containment structure.


                                              Edwin S. Lyman, Ph.D.
                                              Director of Nuclear Power Safety
                                              Union of Concerned Scientists
